profile.campus: The Dalles, Wasco County, Oregon (Google's original self-built data center campus)
profile.address: West 2nd Street, The Dalles, Wasco County, Oregon, 97058
profile.reading: This building is one of two data center structures Google has built along West 2nd Street on its original Dalles campus, the site where Google began constructing its first self-operated data center in 2006. Google's own data center locations page lists Oregon among its earliest and most significant US data center states, and the company has stated it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon infrastructure since 2006, spread across the multiple buildings that now make up the Dalles campus. Google began construction of a fourth building at the site in 2015, expanding beyond the original two-building footprint reflected in OpenStreetMap's mapping of this location. Google chose The Dalles for its location along the Columbia River, which provided both hydroelectric power access from Bonneville Power Administration dams and river water Google has used for cooling, a choice that later became the subject of a long-running local dispute. Fortune's longform reporting and Oregon Public Broadcasting have both covered tension between Google and the City of The Dalles over how much of the city's water rights the data center campus consumes for cooling, with some residents quoted describing the company's local reputation shifting over nearly two decades of expansion. The Dalles campus predates Google's newer Taylor Lake data center project nearby, and this registry treats the original West 2nd Street buildings and the Taylor Lake buildings as distinct facilities despite sharing the same Wasco County campus and operator. Google has not disclosed which specific building on West 2nd Street this OSM-mapped structure corresponds to, nor its individual power capacity or floor area, consistent with Google's general practice of reporting investment and jobs figures only at the state or metro level rather than per building. This registry records the state-level $7 billion Oregon investment figure as regional context rather than attributing it to any single building, and flags county assessor parcel records as the next real research step for building-specific square footage.

sources.title: Fortune longform on the Google/Dalles water dispute

profile.capacity_note: not published at individual building level
profile.facility_note: Part of Google's original West 2nd Street data center campus in The Dalles, one of two similarly unlabeled buildings OpenStreetMap contributors have mapped at this location.

profile.regional_context: Oregon has no state sales tax, and Wasco County's enterprise zone program has abated local property taxes on Google's Dalles investment for years at a time under agreements renewed as each new building comes online, a structure local officials credit with anchoring Google's continued expansion at the site since 2006.

reading.body:
Google does not publish the power capacity or square footage of individual buildings at its Dalles campus, only aggregate investment figures for the state of Oregon. The facility sits in Wasco County as part of a campus begun in 2006 that Google has described as its first data center built and operated by the company itself. Google reports more than $7 billion invested in Oregon since the site's opening, with construction of a fourth building begun in 2015.

Among the 133 facilities mapped in Oregon, only 8 operators publish individual megawatt figures. This campus cannot be ranked against others in the state by capacity because Google does not disclose it. Statewide, published capacity totals 156.6 MW across eight facilities. The absence of published figures for this site means its actual role in Oregon's data center footprint is unknown in quantitative terms.

The historical significance of the Dalles campus to Google's infrastructure strategy is documented in the company's own disclosures. Whether the campus matters to current AI scaling depends on unpublished facts: the operating power draw of each building, the age and architecture of the existing infrastructure, and Google's upgrade plans. None of these are in the public record.
